The **threshold wavelength** is the longest wavelength that can just eject an electron,
and the work function is inversely proportional to it.
**Step 1 — write the relation.** At threshold the photon energy exactly equals the work
function:
W = hc/λ₀ ✓
so **W ∝ 1/λ₀**.
**Step 2 — read the two thresholds.** The first emitter needs light of **300 nm** and
the second manages with **600 nm**, so these are their threshold wavelengths.
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
W₁/W₂ = λ₀₂/λ₀₁
= 600/300
= **2 : 1** ✓
**Why the longer threshold means the smaller work function.** A longer wavelength carries
**less** energy per photon ✓ If a metal can be worked by feeble 600 nm photons, its
electrons must be held less tightly than those of a metal needing 300 nm photons.
**The numbers, using hc = 1240 eV nm.**
W₁ = 1240/300 = **4·13 eV**
W₂ = 1240/600 = **2·07 eV** ✓
and their ratio is exactly **2 : 1** ✓
**What those values correspond to.** A work function near 2 eV is typical of **caesium**
or other alkali metals, which respond to visible light; around 4 eV is typical of
**zinc** or **aluminium**, which need ultraviolet ✓
**Why wavelength and energy run opposite ways.** E = hc/λ, so the relation is
**inverse** ✓ Doubling the wavelength halves the photon energy - which is why the ratio
of work functions is the **reciprocal** of the ratio of wavelengths, and why answering
1 : 2 is the commonest slip.
**A practical consequence.** A photocell made of the second material responds to red
light; one made of the first needs ultraviolet ✓ This is why photocells are chosen by
work function to suit the light they must detect.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 2** ✗ inverts the ratio. **4 : 1** ✗ and **1 : 4** ✗
would follow from squaring it, as if energy went as 1/λ² ✓
∴ 2 : 1.

The stopping potential is the voltage that just removes the **maximum kinetic energy** of
the photoelectrons.
**Step 1 — write the condition.**
eV₀ = ½mv²_max
**Step 2 — rearrange to use the specific charge.** Dividing through by m:
V₀ = v²_max/[2(e/m)] ✓
which needs only the **ratio** e/m, which is what is given.
**Step 3 — substitute.**
V₀ = (1·2 x 10⁶)²/[2 x 1·8 x 10¹¹]
= 1·44 x 10¹²/(3·6 x 10¹¹)
= **4 V** ✓
**Why the specific charge is enough.** Both the energy ½mv² and the work eV₀ contain the
electron's properties, and in the ratio only **e/m** survives ✓ Neither e nor m is
needed separately - a neat feature of this kind of problem.
**A check with the actual constants.**
½mv² = ½(9·1 x 10⁻³¹)(1·44 x 10¹²) = **6·55 x 10⁻¹⁹ J**
V₀ = 6·55 x 10⁻¹⁹/(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹) = **4·1 V** ✓ agreeing with the answer, the small
difference coming from the rounded specific charge given in the question (the true value
is 1·76 x 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹).
**What the stopping potential means physically.** The collector is made **negative**
enough that even the fastest photoelectron is turned back just as it arrives ✓ The
photocurrent then falls to zero, and the voltage at which that happens measures the
maximum kinetic energy directly.
**What it depends on.** Only on the **frequency** of the light and the metal's work
function, through
eV₀ = hν − φ ✓
Not on the intensity: brighter light ejects **more** electrons but none of them faster.
**Reading the distractors.** **2 V** ✗ would need v = 8·5 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹, **3 V** ✗ needs
1·04 x 10⁶, and **6 V** ✗ needs 1·47 x 10⁶ ✓ Substituting each candidate back into
v = √(2(e/m)V₀) checks it at once.
∴ 4.

De Broglie's relation makes momentum **inversely proportional** to wavelength, so the
graph is a rectangular hyperbola.
**Step 1 — write the relation.**
λ = h/p
so
**p = h/λ** ✓
**Step 2 — identify the curve.** With h a constant, p ∝ 1/λ ✓ A plot of p against λ is
therefore a **rectangular hyperbola**: falling steeply at small λ, flattening towards
the axis at large λ, and never touching either axis.
**Step 3 — match to the figures.** The fourth graph shows exactly that shape - a
decreasing curve that is **concave upwards** and asymptotic to both axes ✓
**Why the other shapes are wrong.**
a **rising straight line** ✗ would mean p ∝ λ - momentum increasing with wavelength, the
opposite of the truth
a **rising curve** ✗ likewise has them increasing together
a **falling straight line** ✗ has the right **direction** but the wrong **form**: a
straight line would cross the λ axis, implying zero momentum at some finite
wavelength ✓ For an inverse relation, p approaches zero only as λ → ∞.
**The test that separates the last two.** At λ = 2λ₀ the momentum must be **exactly
half** its value at λ₀ ✓ A straight line cannot do that for every pair of points; only
a hyperbola can.
**A numerical illustration.** For an electron:
λ = 1 Å: p = 6·63 x 10⁻³⁴/10⁻¹⁰ = **6·63 x 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹**
λ = 2 Å: **3·32 x 10⁻²⁴** ✓ halved
λ = 4 Å: **1·66 x 10⁻²⁴** ✓ halved again - the hyperbolic fall.
**How to make the graph a straight line.** Plot p against **1/λ** ✓ That gives a line
through the origin of slope h - which is how Planck's constant is measured from
diffraction data.
**Why this relation matters.** It applies to **every** particle, not just electrons ✓ A
cricket ball has a de Broglie wavelength too, about 10⁻³⁴ m - far too small to show any
wave behaviour, which is why the effect was discovered only with electrons.
∴ the fourth graph - the hyperbola.

Write Einstein's equation twice and eliminate the work function.
**Step 1 — write the two cases.**
with wavelength λ: 3eV_s = hc/λ − φ ... (i)
with wavelength 2λ: eV_s = hc/(2λ) − φ ... (ii)
**Step 2 — subtract (ii) from (i).**
2eV_s = hc/λ − hc/(2λ)
= **hc/(2λ)**
so
**eV_s = hc/(4λ)**
**Step 3 — substitute back into (ii) to find φ.**
hc/(4λ) = hc/(2λ) − φ
φ = hc/(2λ) − hc/(4λ)
= **hc/(4λ)**
**Step 4 — convert the work function to a threshold wavelength.**
φ = hc/λ₀
hc/λ₀ = hc/(4λ)
**λ₀ = 4λ** ✓
**Why the threshold is so much longer than either wavelength used.** The work function
turns out to be only a quarter of the energy of the λ photon ✓ so light of up to four
times that wavelength still carries enough energy to free an electron.
**A check with numbers.** Take λ = 200 nm, so hc/λ = 6·2 eV:
φ = 6·2/4 = **1·55 eV**
at 200 nm: KE_max = 6·2 − 1·55 = **4·65 eV**, so V_s = 4·65 V
at 400 nm: KE_max = 3·1 − 1·55 = **1·55 eV**, so V_s = 1·55 V ✓
and 4·65 is exactly **three times** 1·55 ✓ matching the 3V_s and V_s of the question.
λ₀ = 1240/1·55 = **800 nm = 4λ** ✓
**Why doubling the wavelength more than halves the stopping potential.** The work
function is subtracted from **both** photon energies ✓ Halving the photon energy from
6·2 to 3·1 eV removes 3·1 eV, but the useful kinetic energy falls from 4·65 to 1·55 - a
drop to a third, not a half. That is the whole content of this question.
**Reading the distractors.** **8λ**, **6λ** and **4λ/3** ✗ each follow from a sign slip
or from equating the wrong pair ✓ Substituting any of them back into the two Einstein
equations fails to give the 3 : 1 ratio of stopping potentials.
∴ 4λ.

Einstein's photoelectric equation contains the frequency and the work function - but no
intensity term at all.
**Step 1 — write the equation.**
KE_max = hν − φ
= hc/λ − φ ✓
**Step 2 — read off what it depends on.**
**frequency ν** ✗ appears directly - higher frequency, more energy
**wavelength λ** ✗ appears through ν = c/λ - the same dependence, inverted
**work function φ** ✗ appears directly - a tightly bound electron emerges with less
**intensity** ✓ **does not appear anywhere**
**Step 3 — conclude.** The maximum kinetic energy is independent of the **intensity** ✓
**What intensity does control.** The **number** of photoelectrons per second, and hence
the **saturation photocurrent** ✓ Brighter light ejects more electrons, but not faster
ones.
**Why this was revolutionary.** Classical wave theory predicted exactly the opposite ✓
A more intense wave should deliver more energy to each electron, so brighter light
should give faster electrons - and there should be a time lag while the energy
accumulated. Neither is observed.
**What the experiments actually show.**
below the threshold frequency, **no** electrons at all, however bright the light ✓
above it, emission is **instantaneous**, within 10⁻⁹ s, however faint ✓
the maximum energy rises **linearly** with frequency, with slope h ✓
All three follow at once if light arrives as **photons**, each interacting with a single
electron - which is what Einstein proposed in 1905 and won the Nobel Prize for.
**The one-photon-one-electron picture.** An electron absorbs one photon of energy hν,
spends φ escaping the surface, and keeps the rest ✓ Doubling the number of photons
doubles the number of such events, but changes nothing about any individual one.
**A worked illustration.** Light of 400 nm (3·1 eV) on a metal of φ = 2·0 eV gives
KE_max = **1·1 eV**, whether the beam is a feeble glimmer or a laser ✓ Only the current
differs.
∴ intensity.

The 3 → 2 photon **just** causes emission, so its energy equals the work function; any
weaker photon will fail.
**Step 1 — find the threshold energy.** Using E_n = −13·6/n² eV:
E₃ = −13·6/9 = **−1·51 eV**
E₂ = −13·6/4 = **−3·40 eV**
ΔE = −1·51 − (−3·40) = **1·89 eV** ✓
Since emission is "just" produced, the work function is **φ = 1·89 eV**.
**Step 2 — compute the energy of each listed transition.**
**2 → 1**: −3·40 − (−13·60) = **10·20 eV** ✓ far above threshold
**3 → 1**: −1·51 − (−13·60) = **12·09 eV** ✓ above
**5 → 2**: −0·54 − (−3·40) = **2·86 eV** ✓ above
**4 → 3**: −0·85 − (−1·51) = **0·66 eV** ✗ **below** threshold
**Step 3 — conclude.** Only the **4 → 3** photon is too feeble, so photoelectric emission
is **not possible** for it ✓
**Why 4 → 3 is the weakest.** The hydrogen levels crowd together as n rises ✓ The gap
between adjacent high levels is tiny compared with the gap down to n = 1 or n = 2, so
transitions among the upper levels give infrared photons of very little energy.
**The energies, laid out.**
E₁ = −13·60, E₂ = −3·40, E₃ = −1·51, E₄ = −0·85, E₅ = **−0·54 eV** ✓
The spacing shrinks rapidly - from 10·2 eV between the first two levels to 0·66 eV
between the third and fourth.
**The corresponding wavelengths.**
4 → 3: 1240/0·66 = **1875 nm** - infrared, the first Paschen line
5 → 2: 1240/2·86 = **434 nm** - visible violet, a Balmer line ✓
**The principle being tested.** The photoelectric effect has a sharp **threshold** ✓
A photon either carries enough energy to free an electron or it does not; no number of
sub-threshold photons will substitute for one above threshold.
**Reading the distractors.** The other three transitions all release **more** than
1·89 eV, so each would eject electrons - with kinetic energies of 8·31, 10·20 and
0·97 eV respectively ✓
∴ from n = 4 to n = 3.

An electron accelerated through V volts has a de Broglie wavelength given by the standard
shortcut **λ = 12·27/√V Å**.
**Step 1 — find the momentum.** The electron gains kinetic energy eV:
½mv² = eV
p = mv = **√(2meV)** ✓
**Step 2 — apply de Broglie's relation.**
λ = h/p
= **h/√(2meV)**
**Step 3 — evaluate the constants.**
λ = 6·63 x 10⁻³⁴/√(2 x 9·1 x 10⁻³¹ x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ x V)
= 1·227 x 10⁻⁹/√V m
= **12·27/√V Å** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute V = 100.**
λ = 12·27/√100
= 12·27/10
= **1·227 Å** ✓
**Why this wavelength is so useful.** 1·227 Å is comparable with the **spacing between
atoms** in a crystal, a few ångström ✓ That is exactly why electrons of around 100 V
diffract from crystals - the basis of the Davisson-Germer experiment and of electron
microscopy.
**The inverse square-root dependence.** λ ∝ 1/√V ✓ so
at 100 V: **1·227 Å**
at 400 V: **0·614 Å** - halved, because V has quadrupled
at 10000 V: **0·123 Å** ✓
Higher accelerating voltages give shorter wavelengths and finer resolution, which is why
electron microscopes run at tens of kilovolts.
**Comparison with light.** Visible light has λ ≈ 5000 Å, some four thousand times
longer ✓ An electron microscope can therefore resolve detail thousands of times finer
than any optical one.
**A caution at high voltages.** Above about 50 kV the electron becomes relativistic and
the simple formula overestimates λ ✓ At 100 V the correction is utterly negligible.
**Reading the distractors.** **12·27 Å** ✗ forgets the √V, giving the value for 1 V.
**0·1227 Å** ✗ and **0·001227 Å** ✗ are the values for 10 kV and 1 MV ✓ A factor-of-ten
error in the voltage shifts the answer by a factor of √10, so checking the power of ten
is essential.
∴ 1.227 Å.
